assumptions: The product remains read-only downstream of the payer's PSP result, and a human at the customer always authorizes or rejects the payment.
The absence of partner access, exception-volume data, pilots, and willingness-to-pay evidence is treated as uncertainty rather than proof of no demand.
The initial beachhead is euro-area multi-bank enterprises or payment bureaus; Poland is not assumed to provide the immediate regulatory wedge before July 2027.
Supplier identity and resolution data remain tenant-specific unless explicit contractual and legal permission supports broader reuse.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A verification result does not resolve the close-match, no-match, or unavailable case, so the gap between regulated messaging and safe supplier-master remediation is real. The insight is useful but already adjacent to incumbent portal and audit functionality.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Fraudulent credit transfers cause large documented losses, users bear most losses, and unresolved beneficiary exceptions can delay or misdirect high-value payments. This provides a strong basis for buyer pain, although exception frequency and incremental willingness to pay beyond a free bank result are unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A tenant subscription plus documented-resolution fee can align with enterprise value without reselling the mandated check. Long partner and security reviews, revenue share, support, low possible exception volume, and third-party data costs threaten margin and payback; all retention and wealth-path assumptions are unvalidated.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Euro-area enterprise AP teams and payment bureaus with complex bulk and multi-bank workflows are a narrow, economically consequential segment. The free PSP service, bulk opt-out, and later Polish deadline reduce the immediately addressable software budget but do not eliminate the operational niche.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: SurePay already has extensive bank coverage, enormous verification volume, thousands of organizational users, APIs, a white-label portal, and audit functionality, while banks such as AIB own the corporate channel. An independent vendor has little basis for segment domination without a privileged AP-platform position.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A trusted exception layer can expand into supplier-master hygiene, change-of-bank-detail controls, payment-bureau workflows, additional banks, and adjacent fraud evidence. Those adjacencies remain security-sensitive and dependent on partner interfaces, but they are commercially coherent.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Tenant-specific supplier aliases, confirmed outcomes, and embedded approval playbooks can create switching costs and improve recommendations. Without lawful cross-tenant learning there is no true network effect, and the incumbent already operates a much broader shared verification graph.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Structured evidence gathering and supplier-record correction can be more useful than a bare verification result. The packet does not establish a material advantage over SurePay's workflow or bank-native portals in fraud reduction, speed, accuracy, auditability, or total cost.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The regulatory rollout forces euro payment workflows to ingest new results and creates a timely integration window. Corporate opt-out, an established provider ecosystem, and Poland's July 2027 deadline make the momentum uneven for this founder's most accessible geography.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The published scheme API is inter-PSP, so a bank, PSP, or AP platform must expose the result contractually. No such relationship exists, and the same gatekeepers can provide or bundle competing exception workflows while retaining the enterprise customer.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder is technically suited to entity resolution and auditable data systems, and a read-only prototype is conceivable within stated time. Bank-grade security, payments counsel, insurance, enterprise integration, false-resolution liability, partner support, and near-ceiling pilot capital materially complicate part-time execution.

main_structural_strength: The workflow sits after a mandatory verification message but before an irreversible human-authorized payment, allowing a well-integrated product to tie supplier-master correction and evidence directly to avoided loss and approval-cycle time.
primary_score_limiter: Essential data access and customer distribution depend on PSP, bank, or AP-platform partners that already control the workflow and can choose an incumbent, bundle the exception layer, or withhold the interface.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: SurePay already supplies bulk APIs, white-label portals, audit-oriented workflow, broad bank connectivity, and massive verification intelligence, and AIB demonstrates that a bank can distribute that corporate workflow natively.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A contractually authorized PSP or AP-platform design partner; paid pilots with measured exception rates and resolution time; proof of fraud-loss or labor reduction beyond the free result; security and legal feasibility; and validated partner costs, gross margin, retention, and enterprise acquisition payback.
highest_value_structural_change: Replace the independent network thesis with a white-label, multi-bank supplier-master remediation module for one AP platform or payment bureau, using that partner's authorized result feeds and distribution to solve cross-bank normalization that individual bank portals do not.
